questions.prompt: What happens when an IFEO Debugger value is set for an executable?
options: Windows blocks that executable from running
Windows launches the specified debugger instead, passing the original executable as an argument
Windows logs every launch of that executable
The executable runs with elevated privileges
questions.explanation: IFEO's Debugger value is a legitimate debugging feature that redirects execution -- the abuse is that the specified 'debugger' can be any program at all.

questions.prompt: Why is the accessibility backdoor (sethc.exe / utilman.exe) especially serious?
options: It requires Domain Admin to plant
Those tools are reachable from the lock screen before authentication, so an IFEO Debugger set to cmd.exe yields a SYSTEM shell with no credentials at all
It only works on domain controllers
questions.explanation: Because Sticky Keys and Ease of Access are invokable pre-authentication, this becomes a standing backdoor -- particularly on any host reachable over RDP.

questions.prompt: Why is AppInit_DLLs still worth checking despite being disabled by default on Secure Boot systems?
options: It is actually enabled by default on all systems
Broadly disabled mechanisms are exactly the ones organizations lack detections for, and older or specially-configured systems still honour it
It cannot be disabled at all
Secure Boot has no effect on it
questions.explanation: Mechanisms assumed dead tend to be unmonitored, and legacy or non-Secure-Boot systems remain vulnerable.

questions.prompt: Why would an attacker set an IFEO Debugger value pointing at a non-existent path for a security product's executable?
options: To make the security product run faster
To prevent that binary from launching at all -- defence evasion rather than persistence
To redirect its logs to the attacker
questions.explanation: Since Windows tries to launch the specified debugger instead, an invalid path means the original executable never runs -- effectively disabling the tool.
